section.title: Limits from motion and approximation
section.p: A speedometer gives an instantaneous reading. But if all we have is a position formula, we first see only average velocities over intervals. The limit is the act of shrinking the interval until the average rate settles toward one number.

figure.caption: The slopes of the secant lines approach the slope of the tangent line at t=2.

subsection.p: The same calculation can be read geometrically. The average velocity over an interval is the slope of a secant line. As the second point moves toward t=2, the secant line approaches a tangent line.
This is why limits are needed before derivatives can be defined. A tangent slope is not usually found from two separated points. It is found by letting one point approach another.

exercise.title: Why is instantaneous velocity a limit of averages?

statement.p: For s(t)=t^2, the average velocity over an interval of width h is 4+h whenever h\neq0. In your own words, why is that average not yet a speedometer reading, and why should shrinking the interval be a better clue to the velocity at the instant t=2?

hint.p: An average still spreads a change over a whole window. The speedometer asks about one instant inside that window. Geometrically, secant slopes are trying to settle toward a tangent slope.

subsection.title: Decimal approximations to a number
subsection.p: Limits do not belong only to motion. They also appear whenever approximations close in on a target.
Chapter 2 used nested intervals to trap \sqrt2:
The left endpoints
approach \sqrt2 from below. The right endpoints approach it from above. Neither finite list equals the whole number \sqrt2, but the approximations can be made as close as desired.
A simpler example is
These numbers approach 2. The error after n decimal places is a power of 10:
The errors approach 0. So the approximations approach 2.

note.title: A limit is a target value for a process
note.p: A number can be approached by decimal approximations. A velocity can be approached by average velocities. A tangent slope can be approached by secant slopes.

subsection.p: The same idea appears in different clothing. The mathematics is the same: errors are forced to become small.

exercise.title: What is a limit a target for?

statement.p: Decimal approximations approach a number, average velocities approach an instantaneous velocity, and secant slopes approach a tangent slope. In your own words, what do these processes have in common, and why is a limit a target value for a process rather than a value read off at the missing input?

hint.p: Each process produces a sequence of errors that we try to force toward zero. The target is what the nearby values are heading toward, whether or not the process is allowed to use the exact center.

statement.p: We write

subsection.p: This definition is still informal because the phrases “as close as desired” and “sufficiently close” have not yet been made precise. Section will do that. For now, the informal definition is enough to compute and interpret many limits.

exercise.title: Why is a limit near a not the same as the value at a?

statement.p: The notation x\to a does not mean x=a. In your own words, why can a function have a limit at a even if f(a) is missing or has been placed somewhere else, and what extra agreement will later be called continuity?

hint.p: A limit watches nearby outputs. The actual assigned height at the point is a separate piece of data. Continuity is the calm case where those two numbers match.

subsection.title: Limits from graphs and tables
subsection.p: A graph can suggest a limit. A table can suggest a limit. But both must be read with care.

exercise.title: What can a table or graph do for a limit?

statement.p: A table of nearby values can suggest a limit, and a graph can suggest that no limit exists. In your own words, why is that evidence useful, and why is it still not a proof?

hint.p: A table checks a few inputs. A graph depends on a window. Algebra will later prove what every nearby value is doing, not only the sampled ones.

subsection.title: What a limit can ignore
subsection.p: The limit
ignores the value f(a). It watches what happens near a.
That means all three situations below are possible.

row.cell: f(a) exists and equals the limit
f(a) exists but differs from the limit
f(a) does not exist, but the limit exists

subsection.p: The first situation is the calm one. The second and third are warning signs. They show why limits must come before continuity.
The next task is practical. Graphs and tables help us guess limits, but calculus needs reliable ways to calculate them. Algebra gives the first tools.
